items.title: [pewresearch.org] Pew projects Muslims will surpass Christians globally by 2035
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center. Both populations are expected to grow, but the Muslim population is projected to increase faster, mainly because Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women. Pew estimates there were 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians in 2020. If current trends continue, the Muslim population will exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population will remain just below 3 billion. The world population is projected to grow 29% over the same period. The report models demographic patterns across 201 countries and territories, including age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching. Its projections do not account for events such as wars, epidemics or natural disasters. By 2070, sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be home to more than half of the world’s Christians, while Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population. Pew’s researchers say the projected growth is largely taking place in countries where each faith is already predominant, rather than reflecting a direct shift from one religion to the other.

items.title: [al-monitor.com] AFP Gaza journalists' film wins Montreal festival's top documentary prize
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

“Inside Gaza,” a 72-minute film following four Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalists reporting from Gaza, won the Best Documentary award and an audience award at Montreal’s Cinemania Film Festival on Nov. 14. The film follows the journalists during the first seven months after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, documenting the risks and difficulties of reporting from a territory largely inaccessible to international media. Directed by Hélène Lam Trong, the documentary draws mainly on footage the journalists shot for AFP and interviews recorded after they left Gaza. AFP Gaza bureau chief Adel Zaanoun accepted the awards in Montreal and dedicated them to journalists killed in the war and those still working there. The film has won other festival awards and is eligible for consideration for the 2027 Oscars.

items.title: [thestar.com] McGill report finds deepfake network spreading false Canada-U.S. trade claims
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. Many focused on Canada’s trade dispute with the United States. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. It appeared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and drew 5.1 million views. The report says the accounts promote misleading claims from both sides of the trade debate, while the network’s operators and purpose remain unknown. Researchers said posting patterns and some accounts’ Chinese-language settings or registrations in China point to activity outside North America, but they could not firmly attribute the network to anyone. The report says the accounts have not been monetized and could be building an audience for later use, testing a tool or operating on behalf of someone seeking to influence Canadians.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] UK court convicts two Iranians in plot targeting dissident journalists
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A jury at Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, on Nov. 12 of assisting an Iranian intelligence service by conducting surveillance on critics of Tehran in Britain. Sepahvand was also convicted of conduct linked to preparing a violent attack; Manesh was acquitted of that separate charge. A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, was acquitted of all charges. The targets included Iran International journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, a founder of UK Lawyers for Israel, and a media production professional. British prosecutors and counterterrorism police said Sepahvand acted under the direction of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) or intermediaries, and that the men were offered rewards for sending information to contacts in Iran. Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in espionage in Britain. Police described the verdicts as the first convictions of Iranian nationals under Britain’s 2023 National Security Act. The court is due to sentence Sepahvand and Manesh at the Old Bailey on Dec. 17.

items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.title: [Macworld] How accurately does the Apple Watch measure your heart rate? We put it to the test
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Macworld

With the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Apple introduced a new health-sensing system. The new energy-efficient LED sensors measure heart rate every five seconds. Heart rate variability is also measured significantly more frequently than before. Macwelt was able to verify this in our review of the Apple Watch Series 12. The watch now measures your pulse every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, and heart rate variability is now recorded every five minutes. The battery still lasts for 24 hours.

This is exciting, because the Apple Watch already had stellar heart-rate tracking. How often and how accurately has the Apple Watch been measuring key health parameters to date? Apple hides the answers to these questions in its support documents. For some measurements, there are no official figures at all. So we took a closer look using the Apple Watch Series 11, which has the same third-gen optical heart rate sensor that was introduced with the Apple Watch Series 6.

How often does the Apple Watch Series 11 measure heart rate?

The answer to this question depends on the situation and the settings on your Apple Watch. In workout mode, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five seconds. The watch also measures your heart rate at this high frequency for the first three minutes after your workout. However, there is also a special setting for long workouts, where the user can activate power-saving mode if required. Apple claims that measurements are taken less frequently in this mode. I recorded a HIIT workout using the Polar H10 chest strap as a reference device. I also started the same workout on the Apple Watch Series 11.

Foundry

The Apple Watch actually measures heart rate every five seconds while the wearer is exercising. Measurements in power-saving mode during a workout also take place every five seconds. However, the system pauses the measurement for several minutes. This means that the heart rate is measured in short intervals every 5 seconds, then the Apple Watch pauses. You can see this on the graph of the heart rates measured during the workout up to the green line: up to that point, the Apple Watch was running in power-saving mode; after that, I switched it off.

Speaking of power-saving mode. If this mode is activated all the time, no background measurements take place, neither of the heart rate nor of heart rate variability. Furthermore, the vital signs data following a recorded night’s sleep lacks the oxygen saturation readings from during the night.

The Apple Watch can also measure your heart rate every second, just like chest straps do during a workout. However, these measurements only occur sporadically: during user-initiated ECG readings and during background HRV measurements. When you launch the ECG app and place your finger on the Digital Crown, the animation on the Watch and the PDF generated afterwards show the heart rate readings for every second. During HRV measurement, too, the Apple Watch records each heart rate over the course of a minute and then uses a specific formula to calculate the time interval between individual heartbeats.

In the background, and particularly at night while you’re asleep, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five minutes. However, the measurements aren’t as regular as they are during exercise. The intervals can vary more significantly when you’re at rest.

I exported and analysed measurements from a sample night using the Health app. For the sake of clarity, the chart above shows only one hour. During six and a half hours of sleep, the Apple Watch took 83 measurements. The average interval between measurements here is 4 minutes 39 seconds, although gaps of 16 minutes or as little as 40 seconds are also possible.

How accurately does the Apple Watch measure heart rate data?

When unveiling the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple claimed that the new smartwatch was the most accurate heart rate fitness tracker on the market. While we can only verify this claim through a single test, older models show that the Apple Watch was already quite accurate when it came to heart rate measurement.

When we tested the Apple Watch Ultra 3, we found that the Ultra’s readings deviated only very slightly from those of the chest strap. I analysed the same HIIT workout described above using the Apple Watch Series 11. The following picture emerges from the progression of the two graphs. On average, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate quite accurately during exercise.

The correlation coefficient between the two measurements–from the Polar H10 and the Apple Watch Series 11–is 0.95. This means the Apple Watch measures quite closely to a chest strap. On average, the two readings differ by just one beat. However, there are outliers: the higher the heart rate, the less accurate the measurement becomes. This can be seen in the line showing heart rates of 160 beats per minute and above. The measurement is also rather inaccurate in power-saving mode, as the Apple Watch can completely miss heart rate spikes due to the sporadic mode.

The new features Apple announced for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are exciting because they effectively turn the entire heart rate measurement algorithm on its head.
